9.2 Safety Tuning, Refusal, Misuse, and Frontier Risk

A course on generative-model safety should begin with the failure it is meant to prevent, not with the metric that happens to be fashionable. Post-training safety methods shape propensities rather than install hard prohibitions. Instruction tuning, preference optimisation, constitutional approaches, filters and refusal policies can reduce harmful outputs, yet attackers may search for jailbreaks and benign users may be over-refused. This distinction matters because the same numerical result can support very different conclusions depending on the deployment context. The relevant question is always conditional: what exactly has been observed, under which assumptions, and which future decision is that evidence supposed to justify? Keeping those three parts together prevents a familiar failure of AI projects, in which a technically correct measurement is gradually retold as a much stronger claim than the experiment ever established.

Consider a model that refuses a straightforward cybersecurity educational question yet can be induced through a multi-step role-play to provide more dangerous assistance. The system has learned a policy imperfectly rather than acquired a formal access-control rule. What makes the example useful is the separation between mechanism and symptom. The visible symptom may be an incorrect answer, an unfair alert, an unsafe action or a privacy leak, but the mechanism can sit in the data pipeline, model, retrieval layer, policy engine, user interface or organisational process. A trustworthy-AI investigation therefore resists the urge to repair the first component that looks suspicious. It reconstructs the path that produced the outcome and asks which intervention would actually break that path.

Instruction tuning, preference optimization, constitutional approaches, classifiers, policy models, and system-level filters can reduce harmful outputs. HarmBench and AILuminate help standardize parts of this evaluation. Yet refusal behavior is itself a trade-off. A system that refuses everything is safe in a narrow sense and useless in practice. A system that answers too freely creates misuse risk. Evaluation should therefore measure both unsafe compliance and inappropriate refusal, under realistic adversarial prompting and benign edge cases.

Frontier developers have introduced capability-triggered governance frameworks for severe risks. OpenAI's Preparedness Framework, Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework differ in details but share a pattern: evaluate advanced capabilities, define thresholds, and require stronger safeguards as risk-relevant capability rises. These frameworks are important experiments in engineering governance. They are also company-defined and should not be confused with independent certification or public regulation.

This also changes how evidence is designed. Evaluate both harmful-compliance and benign-refusal rates, test adaptive attacks, apply use-case-specific filters, restrict dangerous tools and data, and escalate controls with capability and consequence. Frontier-risk evaluations should be treated as empirical risk indicators with uncertainty, not as proofs of absence. Evidence should be collected at the level at which a claim can be falsified. Averages are helpful for orientation, but engineers need slices, counterexamples, traces, thresholds and failure cases when those are what determine whether authority should be granted. The most valuable evaluation is often not the one with the most samples; it is the one that can cause the team to change a release decision because it directly exercises an assumption on which the system depends.

A useful discipline is to separate capability evidence from assurance evidence. Capability evidence asks whether the system can perform a task under some conditions. Assurance evidence asks whether it can be relied upon for a specified purpose, which also requires information about failure behavior, detection, containment, human response and change over time. The distinction becomes increasingly important for general-purpose models because impressive competence on difficult benchmarks can coexist with surprisingly simple failures. A trustworthy system needs an account of both sides of that jagged performance profile.

9.3 System Cards, Model Updates, and Open Weights

The first useful move is to make documentation and release context concrete. Model cards and system cards are most useful when they state the system’s intended use, evaluated conditions, limitations, safety controls and known failure modes. They become weak when treated as marketing summaries detached from versioned evidence. This distinction matters because the same numerical result can support very different conclusions depending on the deployment context. The relevant question is always conditional: what exactly has been observed, under which assumptions, and which future decision is that evidence supposed to justify? Keeping those three parts together prevents a familiar failure of AI projects, in which a technically correct measurement is gradually retold as a much stronger claim than the experiment ever established.

Consider an application silently moving to a new foundation-model checkpoint whose capability improves but tool-calling behavior and refusal boundaries change. A static card written six months earlier no longer describes the deployed object. What makes the example useful is the separation between mechanism and symptom. The visible symptom may be an incorrect answer, an unfair alert, an unsafe action or a privacy leak, but the mechanism can sit in the data pipeline, model, retrieval layer, policy engine, user interface or organisational process. A trustworthy-AI investigation therefore resists the urge to repair the first component that looks suspicious. It reconstructs the path that produced the outcome and asks which intervention would actually break that path.

Model cards helped normalize structured documentation of intended use, evaluation, and limitations. For modern generative products, system cards need to go further. They should record the complete configuration that produced the evidence: base model, post-training, tools, retrieval, safety layers, important prompts or policy logic, versions, access modes, evaluation suites, known failures, and operational monitoring. Otherwise, the documented artifact is not the artifact users encounter.

Foundation-model APIs can change even when the application code remains stable. A new model snapshot may improve coding and worsen a particular refusal behavior; a new safety policy may change outputs; a new context window may alter retrieval dynamics. Version pinning, release qualification, regression suites, and change notices are therefore part of trustworthy deployment. When version pinning is impossible, the application must assume that the underlying component is dynamic and monitor it accordingly.

Open-weight models increase inspectability, local control, customization, and scientific access, but they also make some centralized safeguards unenforceable after distribution. Closed APIs allow providers to monitor use and update mitigations, while creating concentration, opacity, and dependency risks. The trustworthy-AI question is not whether openness is inherently safer or more dangerous. It is which risks can be controlled by which actor after the model is released, and how the governance architecture allocates responsibility.

This also changes how evidence is designed. Couple documentation to version control and assurance claims, record provider and application-level changes, and distinguish model properties from system properties. For open-weight releases, account for the fact that downstream actors can remove safeguards, fine-tune behavior and construct different harnesses. 10. Trustworthy Agents and Multi-Agent Systems
segments.translation: 10. Agenți și sisteme multiagent demne de încredere

segments.source: Engineering question: What changes when an AI system can remember, decide, call tools and alter the world before a human reviews the result?

An agent is not simply a language model with a larger prompt. It is a feedback loop: observe, update state, plan, call a tool, observe the consequence and continue. Every turn can expand the consequences of an earlier error, and memory can preserve malicious or mistaken information across time. The International AI Safety Report 2026 highlights heightened reliability risks for agents and additional risks from multi-agent interaction. Meridian now crosses the line from answering questions to preparing actions, making authority and containment the central design variables.
10.1 Actions, Tools, Memory, and Authority

The first useful move is to make agent architecture concrete. Agentic risk grows with a combination of autonomy, persistence, tool access and authority. The same planning error has different consequences in a read-only sandbox, an email client and a payment system. This distinction matters because the same numerical result can support very different conclusions depending on the deployment context. The relevant question is always conditional: what exactly has been observed, under which assumptions, and which future decision is that evidence supposed to justify? Keeping those three parts together prevents a familiar failure of AI projects, in which a technically correct measurement is gradually retold as a much stronger claim than the experiment ever established.

Consider an assistant that writes a draft email versus one that can send messages, modify access permissions and execute purchases. Capability benchmarks may be identical, but the second system has a much larger blast radius. What makes the example useful is the separation between mechanism and symptom. The visible symptom may be an incorrect answer, an unfair alert, an unsafe action or a privacy leak, but the mechanism can sit in the data pipeline, model, retrieval layer, policy engine, user interface or organisational process. A trustworthy-AI investigation therefore resists the urge to repair the first component that looks suspicious. It reconstructs the path that produced the outcome and asks which intervention would actually break that path.

A useful mental model is that an agent repeatedly maps its current state into an action. The state includes user intent, conversation history, retrieved data, tool results, memory, permissions, and intermediate artifacts. Trustworthy design must control both what information enters the state and what actions the policy is allowed to select. This is why memory and tool permissions are part of the trust boundary.

Agent benchmarks are moving from isolated tool calls toward long-horizon realistic tasks. AgencyBench, published at ACL 2026, explicitly targets multiple core agent capabilities across real-world scenarios and very long contexts. A 2026 review of agentic evaluation identifies a persistent deployment gap: benchmark success does not adequately capture safety compliance, maintainability, cost, and process quality. Trustworthy-agent evaluation should therefore inspect the path as well as the outcome.

A final answer can be correct even if the agent violated policy while obtaining it. Conversely, an agent can fail the task because it correctly refused an unauthorized action. Process metrics should therefore include permission compliance, policy violations, unnecessary tool calls, recovery from tool failure, provenance of intermediate state, human-intervention rate, cost, and the reversibility of actions.

This also changes how evidence is designed. Model the agent as a stateful control loop, enumerate tools and side effects, classify actions by reversibility and consequence, scope memory by task, and allocate authority progressively. Separate proposing, validating, approving and executing when stakes justify the latency. Evidence should be collected at the level at which a claim can be falsified. Averages are helpful for orientation, but engineers need slices, counterexamples, traces, thresholds and failure cases when those are what determine whether authority should be granted. The most valuable evaluation is often not the one with the most samples; it is the one that can cause the team to change a release decision because it directly exercises an assumption on which the system depends.

A useful discipline is to separate capability evidence from assurance evidence. Capability evidence asks whether the system can perform a task under some conditions. Assurance evidence asks whether it can be relied upon for a specified purpose, which also requires information about failure behavior, detection, containment, human response and change over time. The distinction becomes increasingly important for general-purpose models because impressive competence on difficult benchmarks can coexist with surprisingly simple failures. A trustworthy system needs an account of both sides of that jagged performance profile.

Dovezile de capabilitate întreabă dacă sistemul poate îndeplini o sarcină în anumite condiții. Dovezile de asigurare întreabă dacă ne putem baza pe el pentru un scop specificat, ceea ce necesită și informații despre comportamentul în caz de eșec, detectare, limitarea efectelor, reacția umană și schimbarea în timp. segments.source: The boundary of the claim must remain visible. Fine-grained permissions reduce consequences but do not ensure good plans. Memory controls can prevent persistence of some attacks while losing useful context. Human approvals can become rubber stamps under volume pressure. This is not pedantry. Learned systems are deployed in open environments, and evidence can expire when data, users, models, prompts, tools or incentives change. Good engineering documentation therefore says not only what passed, but what was not tested, what assumptions make the result meaningful, what observations would contradict it and what change would force the evidence to be collected again.

Agent systems need comparable delegation semantics. The user should be able to delegate a goal without implicitly delegating every action that might help achieve it. This requires scoped permissions, action classes, monetary and resource limits, time bounds, and escalation rules. Natural-language intent can help choose a plan, but authorization should be represented outside the model in a form that can be enforced deterministically.

Persistent memory is often treated as a usability feature, yet from an assurance perspective it is a long-lived data store that can contain errors, secrets, outdated preferences, adversarial content, or inferred sensitive information. Memories should therefore carry provenance, scope, confidence where meaningful, creation time, update history, and expiration or review rules. An agent should distinguish user-stated facts from model inferences and temporary task state from durable memory. Without those distinctions, a hallucination can become a permanent premise for future action.

There is also an organisational dimension. A control that exists in a design document but is routinely bypassed is not an effective control; a human approval that receives no useful evidence is not independent oversight; a red-team finding that cannot block a release is not a meaningful safety signal. Trustworthiness becomes real only when measurements are connected to authority. This is why the course repeatedly returns to owners, escalation, rollback, incident review and evidence freshness alongside model metrics.
segments.translation: Există și o dimensiune organizațională. O măsură de control care există într-un document de proiectare, dar este ocolită în mod curent, nu este eficientă; o aprobare umană care nu primește dovezi utile nu reprezintă supraveghere independentă; o constatare red-team care nu poate bloca o lansare nu reprezintă un semnal de siguranță semnificativ. Caracterul demn de încredere devine real numai când măsurările sunt conectate la autoritate. De aceea, cursul revine constant la responsabili, escaladare, revenirea la o versiune anterioară, analiza incidentelor și actualitatea dovezilor, alături de metricile modelului.

segments.source: For Meridian, it may search documents and prepare procurement recommendations automatically, but sending a vendor communication remains a separately authorised transition. Memory stores provenance and expiry so that old conclusions do not silently become permanent facts. The running system is deliberately ordinary rather than futuristic. Its importance lies in how small product decisions accumulate: adding a repository changes privacy assumptions; adding a tool changes the threat model; adding memory changes persistence; adding autonomy changes the cost of an error. The same pattern occurs in production AI systems across domains. Architecture and governance determine whether a model weakness remains a recoverable inconvenience or becomes a consequential failure.

The engineering takeaway is therefore deliberately conservative. Do not ask a method to establish more than it can. Combine heterogeneous evidence when failure mechanisms differ, preserve counter-evidence instead of averaging it away, and make safe fallback part of the normal design rather than an emergency afterthought. Trust is a human attitude; trustworthy engineering is the work of making reliance inspectable, bounded and revisable.
segments.translation: Concluzia inginerească este, așadar, intenționat prudentă. Nu cereți unei metode să stabilească mai mult decât poate. Combinați dovezi eterogene când mecanismele de eșec diferă, păstrați dovezile contrare în loc să le estompați prin mediere și includeți alternativa sigură de rezervă în proiectarea normală, nu ca pe o soluție de urgență adăugată ulterior. Încrederea este o atitudine umană; ingineria demnă de încredere presupune munca de a face utilizarea unui sistem inspectabilă, limitată și revizuibilă.

segments.source: A second way to reason about actions, tools, memory, and authority is through counterfactual deployment review. Imagine that the system fails tomorrow in a way that is costly but entirely plausible. Which log would explain the event? Which test should have anticipated it? Which component could have contained it? Which person had authority to reduce exposure before the incident? Working backwards from those questions exposes assurance gaps that are invisible in a model-centric review. It also turns abstract principles into engineering requirements: observability, provenance, reversibility and clear ownership are not administrative extras; they are mechanisms for learning from uncertainty without allowing every failure to become a crisis.

The strongest teams also distinguish absence of evidence from evidence of absence. If a red team did not discover a failure, that is evidence about the search that was performed, not a proof that the failure is impossible. If a subgroup has too few examples to estimate performance, reporting the aggregate score does not resolve the uncertainty. If a formal verifier proves one invariant, it does not certify properties outside the formal model. This epistemic discipline may look modest, but it is one of the most important differences between trustworthy engineering and assurance theater.
segments.translation: Cele mai solide echipe disting și absența dovezilor de dovada absenței. Dacă o echipă red-team nu a descoperit un eșec, aceasta oferă dovezi despre căutarea efectuată, nu o dovadă că eșecul este imposibil. Dacă un subgrup are prea puține exemple pentru estimarea performanței, raportarea scorului agregat nu rezolvă incertitudinea. Dacă un verificator formal demonstrează un invariant, el nu certifică proprietăți aflate în afara modelului formal. Această disciplină epistemică poate părea modestă, dar este una dintre cele mai importante diferențe dintre ingineria demnă de încredere și simulacrul de asigurare.

10.2 Agent Hijacking, Long Horizons, and Multi-Agent Failure

The first useful move is to make agent-specific failure modes concrete. Indirect prompt injection can hijack an agent through content it was asked to process. Long horizons amplify small errors because plans depend on earlier state, while multiple agents can propagate correlated mistakes, miscoordinate or exploit one another’s outputs as if independent. This distinction matters because the same numerical result can support very different conclusions depending on the deployment context. The relevant question is always conditional: what exactly has been observed, under which assumptions, and which future decision is that evidence supposed to justify? Keeping those three parts together prevents a familiar failure of AI projects, in which a technically correct measurement is gradually retold as a much stronger claim than the experiment ever established.

Consider a browsing agent encountering a malicious webpage that requests secret exfiltration, then passing a compromised summary to a second agent that assumes the first agent has verified it. Division of labour has multiplied confidence without creating independence. What makes the example useful is the separation between mechanism and symptom. The visible symptom may be an incorrect answer, an unfair alert, an unsafe action or a privacy leak, but the mechanism can sit in the data pipeline, model, retrieval layer, policy engine, user interface or organisational process. A trustworthy-AI investigation therefore resists the urge to repair the first component that looks suspicious. It reconstructs the path that produced the outcome and asks which intervention would actually break that path.
